hypothesis: I will reproduce the FM baseline by writing a full training loop that imports `FM` from `baseline.py`, trains with the same hyperparameters (k=16, lr=0.001, l2=1e-6, batch_size=8192, patience=4), and evaluates on the validation split. The expected outcome is a validation primary of ~0.6016 (within ±0.002 noise floor). This iteration establishes the working pipeline that future improvements will build on.

I want to understand the data distribution to guide feature engineering and modeling choices. Specifically: (1) how many users have positive labels in validation (affects nDCG@5 vs GAUC tradeoffs), (2) the distribution of impression counts per user in validation, (3) which features have the most variance within a user's candidate set (since only within-user variation matters), and (4) the temporal drift in long_view rates across the train/valid windows.

Combining a 10-seed ensemble with within-user rank averaging and a Bayesian-smoothed per-video long_view rate feature (bucketed, computed from train history only) will improve validation primary by at least 0.002 above the 0.6016 baseline.
mechanism: Rank averaging over 10 seeds reduces variance in the within-user ordering, directly improving GAUC and nDCG@5. The smoothed video CTR bucket adds a learned prior for video quality that varies across videos shown to the same user, giving the FM additional signal beyond the raw video embedding. Both effects are additive because they operate on different sources of variance.

evidence.task_structure: With ~5 impressions per user, small ranking errors dominate the metric. Ensembling reduces those errors. The smoothed CTR feature varies across items shown to the same user (unlike user-level features which cancel out), so it contributes real signal.
evidence.previous_experiments: Prior runs: 5-seed ensemble gave 0.60420 (+0.0026 over baseline); smoothed video CTR gave +0.0008; together they account for +0.0024 of a best-ever +0.0025. 10 seeds should push further given monotonic improvement with ensemble size.

hypothesis: Replacing pointwise BCE with BPR pairwise loss (sampling positive-negative pairs within the same user per mini-batch) will improve GAUC because the loss directly maximizes the probability that a positive item is ranked above a negative item for the same user
mechanism: GAUC is the average within-user AUC: it measures how often a positive item is ranked above a negative item for the same user. BPR's objective is exactly -log(sigmoid(score_pos - score_neg)) for same-user pairs, which is the continuous relaxation of this ranking criterion. Pointwise BCE treats each impression independently and does not directly optimize the pairwise ordering. BPR should improve GAUC specifically, which is half of the primary metric.

evidence.task_structure: With only ~5 impressions per user and GAUC being the primary metric, within-user pairwise ordering is exactly what matters. The model sees ~1.75 positives per user on average, giving ~3-4 positive-negative pairs per user to train on.
evidence.previous_experiments: Prior runs table shows ranking objective: 28 attempts, 5 accepted (17%), median delta -0.00138, best delta +0.0026. The best delta of +0.0026 is well above the noise floor. Our current node is at +0.0014, so there's room to improve.
evidence.literature: No directly relevant search results returned for BPR-FM combination; implementing from first principles based on BPR formulation (Rendle et al. 2009).

proposed_change: Replace pointwise BCE training with BPR pairwise training: for each mini-batch, group rows by user, sample one positive and one negative per user (skip users with no contrast), compute FM scores for both, apply BPR loss -mean(log(sigmoid(z_pos - z_neg))), and backpropagate through the FM embedding structure manually with Adam updates. Keep 10-seed ensemble with rank averaging and the smoothed video CTR feature.
expected_result: Improvement of +0.002 to +0.004 in validation primary, mainly through GAUC improvement from 0.669 to 0.672+
falsification_condition: If VAL_PRIMARY does not improve by at least 0.002 over node 2's 0.6030, or if GAUC does not increase substantially, the hypothesis is wrong

risks.leakage: None — BPR only uses the same features and labels as before, just in a pairwise fashion within users
risks.overfitting: BPR with few pairs per user could overfit to training user preferences; mitigated by L2 regularization and early stopping on validation primary
risks.runtime: Pairwise sampling within users per mini-batch adds overhead, but with ~1.14M rows and only ~5 pairs/user average, should still be manageable within 25 minutes

Add per-author Bayesian-smoothed CTR bucket: would add signal but prior analysis shows static video-function features barely help since video_id embedding already captures it; ceiling ~0.0005

The prior best-ever was ~0.6041 with 5 seeds + same features, suggesting our individual models are weaker. The pointwise BCE loss is a proxy for ranking, not the actual objective. BPR directly optimizes within-user pairwise ranking, which is exactly what GAUC measures.

hypothesis: Adding a Bayesian-smoothed per-author long_view rate feature (bucketed into 10 quantile bins, computed from train rows only) on top of the existing per-video CTR feature and 10-seed rank-averaging ensemble will improve validation primary by approximately +0.0008
mechanism: Author-level engagement rate aggregates across all videos by that author, providing a smoothed prior that varies within a user's impression list (different videos in the same session may come from different authors with different historical engagement rates). The FM can learn that high-engagement authors predict long_view, and this signal is orthogonal to the per-video CTR bucket since it aggregates at the author level rather than video level.

evidence.task_structure: Within-user ranking requires features that vary across the videos shown to the same user. Author ID varies across a user's list (multiple different authors can appear), and author-level engagement rate provides a smoothed signal. With ~3500 authors and ~5 impressions/user, author variation within a session is common.
evidence.previous_experiments: Node 2 tested per-video CTR bucket (+0.0014 overall). The findings note explicitly states 'Bayesian-smoothed per-video and per-author long_view rate, bucketed: +0.0008' and 'those two together account for +0.0024 of a best-ever +0.0025, and they compose'. Node 2 implemented only the video half; this adds the author half.
evidence.literature: Not searched this iteration — the mechanism is directly supported by prior run measurements cited in the findings section.

hypothesis: Reweighting training rows by inverse user frequency (so each user contributes equally to gradient regardless of how many training rows they have) will improve GAUC by better matching the training distribution to the per-user-equal evaluation metric
mechanism: Training with equal BCE per row means users with 200 training impressions dominate the gradient 40x more than users with 5 impressions. GAUC averages AUC equally across users. By sampling rows proportionally to 1/user_count (normalized), every user contributes equally to each epoch's gradient, which aligns the optimization objective with the evaluation objective and may improve calibration for low-activity users who constitute a large fraction of eval users

evidence.task_structure: Eval has ~5 impressions/user mean, but training has ~44/user mean. 'Mean(GAUC)' weights each user's AUC equally regardless of activity level. There is an inherent mismatch between uniform-row BCE training and per-user-equal GAUC evaluation.
evidence.previous_experiments: No prior node tested sampling reweighting. Node 3 tried a ranking objective (BPR) and regressed, but that was a fundamentally different objective — this keeps BCE and only changes the sampling distribution.
evidence.literature: Searched 'user frequency reweighting recommendation ranking optimization' — returned neural ranking and GNN papers that did not directly address this mechanism. Not citing.

proposed_change: Precompute per-user training row counts, build a sampling probability array proportional to 1/count (normalized to sum=1), then use np.random.choice with these probabilities to construct each batch instead of sequential shuffled iteration. This oversamples underrepresented users and undersamples heavy users, matching training to the per-user-equal GAUC structure.
expected_result: VAL_PRIMARY improvement of +0.002 to +0.005 over current best 0.6039
falsification_condition: VAL_PRIMARY <= 0.6039 + 0.002 = 0.6059 after running would indicate the distributional mismatch is not the limiting factor, or that the reweighting hurts by throwing away signal from dense users

risks.leakage: None — weights computed from training row counts only, no future information
risks.overfitting: Low — reweighting reduces heavy-user dominance; could potentially hurt if heavy users have richer, more generalizable signal, but this would show as a regression rather than a false positive
risks.runtime: Slightly slower due to weighted np.random.choice instead of sequential batching, but same number of gradient steps; should be within 25-minute limit
